document.title: Afghanistan: Ethnic Diversity and Dissidence
document.publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), Afghanistan: Lessons from the Last War
document.note: CIA report on ethnic divisions within Afghanistan and the impact of Soviet policy in leading disparate groups to oppose the Soviet client state.

organizations.name: Taraki regime
organizations.notes: Pro-Soviet government installed in April 1978. Its land reform, literacy and secularization programs provoked the tribal insurgency, and its purges hit Pashtun families.

organizations.name: Karmal regime
organizations.notes: Soviet-backed government installed after the Soviet invasion. The text says it sought to broaden its base and slow radical social programs.

organizations.name: Soviet Union
organizations.notes: Soviet troops are described as visibly present in Afghanistan. The invasion is said to have fulfilled the population's worst fears.

organizations.name: Afghan Army
organizations.notes: Suffered increased desertions to Pashtun guerrilla forces before the Soviet invasion. It regularly recruits Hazaras.

organizations.name: Pashtun tribal insurgents
organizations.notes: Responsible for most of the insurgency since April 1978, but old tribal rivalries prevent much cooperation.

organizations.name: Durrani
organizations.notes: Pashtun tribe whose families have ruled Afghanistan since unification in the 18th century. It has at least a million members.

organizations.name: Ghilzai
organizations.notes: Large Pashtun tribe of at least a million members.

organizations.name: Yusufzai
organizations.notes: Large Pashtun tribe of at least a million members.

organizations.name: Kuchis
organizations.notes: Nomads of several ethnic groups, 2 to 4 million in number. They trade between Afghanistan and Pakistan and are hostile to settlement and censuses.

organizations.name: Uzbek
organizations.notes: Ethnic group living north of the Hindu Kush on the plain of the Amu Darya; Sunni; mix of Turko-Mongol peoples; largely farmers, merchants and artisans. Described as having given up tribal affiliations and nomadism.

organizations.name: Tajik
organizations.notes: Second-largest ethnic group; scattered nationwide with concentrations in the east and west; mostly Sunni, some Shia; not tribal. Described as tenant farmers and laborers.

organizations.name: Hazara
organizations.notes: Shia ethnic group; homeland Hazarajat; speak Hazaragi; often recruited into the Afghan Army.

organizations.name: Chahar Aimak
organizations.notes: Ethnic group north and west of the Hazara; four main tribal subdivisions; Sunni; Farsi dialect with Turkic loan words; partly semi-nomadic.

organizations.name: Turkmen
organizations.notes: Turkic, Sunni, pastoral group in the northwest; breeders of Karakul sheep; numbers increased in the 1920s with refugees from Soviet collectivization.

organizations.name: Baluchi
organizations.notes: Nomadic Sunni Iranian-language speakers in the sparsely populated southern borderlands; related to Baluchi settled south of Herat.

organizations.name: Brahui
organizations.notes: Dravidian-language group in southern Afghanistan; farmers and nomads.

organizations.name: Nuristanis
organizations.notes: Eastern mountain people, formerly Kafirs; converted to Sunni Islam after 19th-century subjugation; resent government interference.

organizations.name: Kizilbash
organizations.notes: Urban Shia group descended from a Turkish garrison left in Kabul by a Persian conqueror in the mid-18th century; well educated, some in government posts.

organizations.name: Kirghiz
organizations.notes: Pastoral Mongoloid Sunni Turkic-speaking people in the Wakhan Corridor.

organizations.name: Pashtun
organizations.notes: Mentioned as a comparison: some Tajik groups are described as aggressive like the Pashtun.

places.name: Afghanistan
places.significance: Subject of the study, a tribal society of some 20 ethnic groups.

places.name: Pakistan
places.significance: Kuchi nomads trade and seek winter labor there. Tribal ethnic ties cross the border.

places.name: Iran
places.significance: Neighbor whose border areas share ethnic ties with Afghan tribes.

places.name: USSR
places.significance: Neighbor with ethnic ties to northern Afghan peoples. It is the sponsor of the Kabul regime.

places.name: Kabul
places.significance: Capital. Its growth is described as Pashtun-favoring and at the expense of provincial Uzbeks and Hazaras.

places.name: Hindu Kush
places.significance: Mountain barrier that dominates central and eastern Afghanistan. Uzbeks and some Tajiks live north of it.

places.name: Hazarajat
places.significance: Hazara homeland in the mountains west of Kabul, almost inaccessible to government authority.

places.name: Badakhshan
places.significance: Northeastern area with a smaller Hazara presence and mountain Tajiks.

places.name: Amu Darya
places.significance: River plain north of the Hindu Kush where Uzbeks live.

places.name: Herat
places.significance: Baluchi villages lie south of it.

places.name: Wakhan Corridor
places.significance: Far northeastern extension inhabited by the Kirghiz.

places.name: Nuristan
places.significance: Eastern mountains home of the Nuristanis, formerly Kafiristan.

events.description: Installation of the pro-Soviet Taraki regime, which began the present tribal insurgency.
Soviet invasion of Afghanistan and installation of Babrak Karmal as President.
Turkmen entered Afghanistan from the north as refugees from Soviet collectivization, increasing their numbers.
Persian conqueror left a Turkish garrison in Kabul, ancestors of the Kizilbash (mid-18th century).
A Persian conqueror left a Turkish garrison in Kabul, ancestors of the Kizilbash.
An Afghan ruler subdued the Nuristanis in the 19th century, converting many to Islam; Kafiristan renamed Nuristan.
Installation of the pro-Soviet Taraki regime; start of tribal insurgency.
Unification of Afghanistan by a Durrani leader in the 18th century.
Forced resettlement of many Pashtuns north of the Hindu Kush in the late 19th century.
Start of the insurgency, largely Pashtun-led, against the Taraki regime and its reform programs.

Resistance to land reform, literacy and secularization programs led to destruction of government offices and assassination of officials, party cadres, teachers and police; up to about 300 Russians, including women and children, were also killed.
Forced resettlement of many Pashtuns north of the Hindu Kush in the late 1800s.

key_claims: The Pashtuns are about half of Afghanistan's population and have long dominated politically, which causes resentment among Uzbeks, Hazaras and other groups.
The insurgency began in 1978 with the pro-Soviet Taraki regime, whose land reform, literacy and secularization programs were seen as attacks on Islam and the tribal structure.
Pashtun tribes account for most of the insurgency, but old tribal rivalries prevent much cooperation.
The Soviet invasion and installation of Babrak Karmal are judged unlikely to end the insurgency, since its basic causes remain.
Taraki, Amin and Karmal were themselves Pashtuns, and the regime's purges hit Pashtun families, fueling a desire for revenge.
Hazaras, being Shia, are traditionally despised and live in the nearly inaccessible Hazarajat.
This chunk is a descriptive ethnography of Afghan minority groups and contains no named individual actors or jihadist networks.
Hazara are the only Afghan ethnic group that is predominantly Shia and are regularly recruited into the Afghan Army.
Uzbeks and Turkmen are Sunni Turkic groups in northern Afghanistan; Turkmen remain pastoral nomads while Uzbeks have largely given up tribal affiliation.
Nuristanis resent government interference and prefer isolation in the eastern mountains.
Kizilbash are an urban Shia group, some in government positions.
